Mr. LEIGHTON MCCARTHY moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 7) to amend the Steamboat Inspection Act. He said : This is the Bill which I introduced last session, I trust hon. members distributed it throughout the community and obtained an expression of opinion upon it from their constituents. It simply increases the standard of engineers and also prevents American tug boats doing business in Canada with engineers who have not obtained certificates from the Canadian government. The same remark applies to dredges. The present Act allows an uncertificated engineer to work in a dredge ; but under this Bill an engineer employed on a dredge must have a certificate from the Dominion government. It also seeks to do away with the perinits which at present may be granted by tbe Department of Marine to men who act as engineers for a season, and creates a fourth class of engineers to whom certificates may he granted, in the event of the owners of steamers being unable to obtain engineers of the 1st, 2nd or 3rd class.

RICHARDSON (South Grey) Mr. Speaker, in rising to second the resolution which has been moved and so ably supported by the hon. member for Huntingdon, (Mr. Maclaren) I recognize the fact that the subject which is brought to the attention of the House is one of a unique character differing from those which ordinarily occupy the attention of the House. It is a question which rises above the din and the dust of ordinary partisan political strife ; one which makes for the highest well-being of this country for the present and for the future. This resolution appeals to our highest instincts. If the cigarette habit is the evil which we believe it is ; it is an evil that demands a prompt and effective remedy. I recognize that the application of a remedy presents difficulties, bpt I believe that the difficulties are not insuperable. I do not believe, that they can prevent legislation doing away with the evil as it at present exists. I myself am a non-user of tobacco in any form. I do not, however, presume to make an attack on the use of tobacco in general, because I recognize that many of my own friends whom I esteem very highly use it, and I have every occasion to respect these gentlemen for their mental and intellectual attainments ; for their good judgment and for their manly qualities. Were I to attack a habit to which these friends of mine are addicted, I might bo regarded as one of those who
Compound for sins they are inclined to
By damning those they have no mind to,
I may be asked, why I should favour legislation not only of a restrictive character,

HOLMES fWest Huron). I think that my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) is slightly astray in some of his conclusions. One of the reasons why the promoters of this legislation and legislation of a similar character-such as the Lord's Day Bill and Liquor Bills-are so very earnest is because they realize that the legislation passed by the provinces is not effective. The provincial legislatures have not the power to entirely prohibit, and the promoters of this Bill, realizing that local re striction has been a failure, desire a Dominion enactment which will absolutely prohibit the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes. It was admitted in the dehate last session, and I think it will be conceded by almost every hon. member, that the cigarette habit is an evil, but I am afraid that we do not realize the full extent of the evil. Let me quote from the figures of the Trade and Navigation Report to show how this pernicious habit is growing. In 1899, 106,000,000 cigarettes were manufactured in this country. In 1900, that number increased to 123,000,000. In 1901, the amount had reached 125,000,000. and in 1002 the manufacture ran up to 138,000.000. And. notwithstanding the agitation which took place in the country and the debate in this House-which, one would suppose, would have had a beneficial effect-we find that during the year 1903 no less a quantity than 178.000,000 cigarettes were manufactured. or an increase of 40,000.000 over the year 1902. When we find this evil thus increasing by leaps and bounds, surely It is our duty to take some action to check it. Every medical man In the House last year,
1 think, adnlitted that the habit of cigarette smoking by our youth was very injurious, and as in the discussion this afternoon that

fact has again been brought out most clearly, I need not take up any time in making any proof in this respect. It does seem to me that the only way by which we can check this habit is by a Dominion Act. It is of the greatest importance to the public welfare that our Canadian youth should develop into the very best manhood. It we thought that our boys were diseased in any way, we would bring them to medical men in order to have, if possible, the disease removed, And if we desire that growing generations should attain their biest development, physically and mentally, we should not hesitate to take the most effective steps to root out this evil, which, if unchecked, will sap their manhood. We have realized the importance of keeping the health of our people free from all taint by preventing undesirable and diseased immigrants coming into the country. It is quite possible that in time immigrants infected with disiease might overcome their ailments and develop into desirable settlers, but the Dominion government, realizing the necessity of safeguarding in every way the health of the community" .have passed legislation absolutely prohibiting the entry of settlers infected with disease. I submit that we are equally bound to take steps to prevent the deterioration of our youth and enable our boys to attain their best development by removing from them this growing evil. We cannot too much commend the exertions of those who are behind this legislation. They are not governed by any sordid motives. They are not actuated by any desire to make dollars and cents out of this movement, but are moved by the bejst motives in the interests of society at large, and I am of the opinion that the best interests of our population demand that legislation of this kind should be placed on our statutes.

I would be sorry to find that the only protest against this proposed legislation should come from the youngest member of this House, the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. La-vergne). I take this opportunity of congratulating him upon bis maiden speech, and I venture to say that if he speaks in future on weightier subjects as well as be has spoken on this subject, be will be a credit to this House and to the country. If I thought this Bill would accomplish the end its advocates have in view, even though it might prevent me smoking a cigarette myself, I would vote for it. But I do not believe it will accomplish this end. I do not believe that legislation of this^ class does good, on the contrary I believe it does harm. Granted that evil is done to the youth of this country by the early smoking of cigarettes ; still I do not think the remedy should be sought for in this House, it should rather be sought for from the parents of these boys, and from teaching in the day schools and Sunday schools. We all know that some of the boys' schools are loosely and laxly managed, and if they are not under proper supervision, worse evils even than cigarette smoking creep in, and are not stamped out until they are taken hold of by a man who has knowledge of and sympathy with youth. Now, I venture to say that if the energy that has been and is being displayed in bringing in Bills of this nature was exercised directly upon the youth of this country, upon their parents, or upon the schools they attend, infinitely better results would be attained. Some of the speakers have referred to the fact that smoking cigarettes produces indigestion. Might I be permitted to suggest to my lady friends who are so interested in this matter, that there is more indigestion produced in Canada, more evil wrought among the youth of this country, by bad cooking than by the use of tobacco. Fortunately, I live in a city constituency and have not to do election campaigning in the country. I make the assertion without hesitation that the best education you can give to the farmers' wives of this country is to teach them how to cook and economize. Not long ago it was my pleasure to attend a meeting in the east end of Toronto, though not in my constituency, where I could make no votes : but there I found two or three ladies had established a school for teaching girls how to cook. They found that a great many girls enter factories at 12 or 14 years of age and marry at 18 or 20 years of age, without having had an opportunity to learn how to cook a potato or to make a cup of tea. Now these ladies are engaged In teaching girls how to do housework, and I understood there were girls there who were to be married within a few months, and they were working as late as the regulations would permit in order to learn how to do a little cooking. I believe you



will benefit the morals of boys more by making them healthy than you will by legislation looking to the prohibition of cigarette smoking. As I said, if I thought this Bill would do any good, if I thought it would have any effect in stopping the smoking of cigarettes by young boys, I would tote for it. But I do not believe in this class of legislation. I do not believe that this Bill if passed would have the effect its supporters expect from it; therefore I must reluctantly vote against it.

I do not propose to offer any extended remarks on the resolution moved by the bon. member for Huntington (Mr. Maclaren). I dq not think it requires any elaborate argument to convince the hon. members of this House and the people of this country, or the majority of them, that evil attends cigarette smoking. To my mind it is apparent wherever we go. We see it in going up and down the streets of our towns and villages, and I do not think that any member of this House would fail to recognize a cigarette smoker wherever he met [DOT] him.
There is no question in my mind that the evil is a very great one in Canada. It is very injurious tp the youth of our land, to growing boys and young men. Notwithstanding the declaration that we have heard to-day from the youngest member of the House who, perhaps, has not yet been a cigarette smoker for any great length of time, I am not prepared to accept the statement of the few. I base my opinion on observation from year to year and the more I have watched young men and boys indulging in this habit the more convinced I am of its) extremely injurious effect upon their health and therefore I have no hesitation in stating to this House that if the resolution is pressed to a division I will vote in support of it. I trust that the resolution will carry if for no other purpose than as a means of educating the people of the country. I think it is well to agitate this question, to draw the attention of our young people to it and point out to them the injurious effects to which they subject themselves by indulging in this, what I call, very pernicious habit.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand it the question now before the chair is simply a formal resolution that we go into Committee of the Whole so as to permit this Bill afterwards to be introduced. I would have no objection to voting for the motion although I would not promise that my vote for that motion would carry with it a vote for the Bill which is brought in unless the Bill is far broader than this resolution. Last session when this matter was brought up, the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) proposed, in connection with the criminal code amendment, what appeared to

me a far better plan of dealing with this evident evil existing in the country to-day>
a plan which I believe would be more sefl' sible because that which is advocated to* day is not in accord with the general send' ment of the people of the country. I do no* believe such legislation would be sufficiently well observed.

This question should be looked upon with great seriousness. It is all very well to say that this is a thing which should be left to parents, but parliament is here to protect the best interests of the country and in safeguarding the welfare of our young men we accomplish that result. Certain people who have not had the good fortune to have children, will describe to you how children should be brought up, but I wish hon. gentlemen to remember, that the young cigarette smokers take good care that their parents do not see them. They not only practice the habit beyond the sight of their parents, but as has been known in the city ol' Halifax, sometimes they steal money to buy cigarettes. The young member (Mr. Lavergne) who has spoken, is not old enough yet to experience the disadvantage of cigarette smoking, but I may tell him that I do not believe that I would have arrived at my ripe old age, had I practiced the use of tobacco in any shape or form. Of course most of us ore old sinners in the use r,f tobacco, and we do not look upon the seriousness of this evil as we should. Reference has been made to good cooking, and I think progress lias been made in that art in the Dominion. I do not think that any of us suffer from bad cooking; perhaps we suffer more from eating too much than from eating too little. It lias also been said that tills oitestion should be dealt with by the different provinces. It is my opinion

that the laws passed by the provinces are not so effectually carried out as those passed by the Dominion parliament. For instance >f the Customs Act and the Inland Revenue Act were provincial Acts, they would be abused to some extent, but because they are enacted by the parliament of Canada they are enforced to the fullest extent. It may be true that we cannot prevent the evil, but there is no doubt that we can reduce it, and if we succeed in bringing the evil to the minimum, then we would be doing service to our country. If we trace the history of those who find their way to our penitentiaries, you will find that many of them had taken to cigarette smoking during their youth, and had gone from bad to worse until at last they disgraced themselves and their families. I shall_ have great pleasure in supporting the motion introduced by the hon. member (Mr. Maa-laren) with which I am heartily in accord. I trust the House will deal with this question in that seriousness which it demands and not treat it flippantly.

served by tbe community. I have always been opposed to prohibition, simply because the experience of mankind shows that if you prohibit a thing, which is not in itself an evil, your law will not be observed, and I think it is always an evil to pass enactments which will not be accepted by the respectable part of the community. If a man can smoke a cigarette with no more , injury to himself than the smoking of a cigar, why should you prevent his indulging in the luxury ? If he prefers a cigarette to a cigar, why should you interfere ? I agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that in our legislation we should try to reach the evil where it exists, and the admitted evil is the smoking of cigarettes by boys. I would prevent boys from smoking, not only cigarettes, but tobacco in any form. I do not hesitate to say that it grates on my feelings to meet a boy ten or twelve years of age with a cigarette in his mouth, and I always wish that the parents would look sharply after such a boy. But to say that because the habit is injurious to a boy, it shall not be allowed a grown-up man, is going altogether too far. In my opinion the peculiar obnoxious feature of the cigarette is its cheapness. Nowadays when a boy gets five cents, instead of spending it on candies, as they used to do when I was a boy, he invests it in a package of cigarettes. How are you going to prevent that ? The remedy, to a large extent, is in the provinces, and I would call the attention of the House to the fact that there is a tendency to-day to come to Ottawa for legislation \ which should not be asked for at Ottawa but in the provincial legislatures. There has been lately a reaction against that practice, and last year we had on the floor of this House several members on both sides protesting against the invasion by the Dominion parliament of the rights of the provinces in the matter of legislation. There are many subjects on which the provinces and the Dominion parliament have a concurrent right to legislate, but in all these matters I think we should endeavour to maintain the autonomy of the provinces. The legislation now sought for exists already to some degree in most of the provinces. There is in most of the provinces legislation dealing with this very evil, but we are told that the laws are ineffective and not enforced. I submit, with all deference to those who arc asking us to legislate, and whose motives I sincerely respect, that if they would see to the enforcement of the provincial laws, the evil could be checked. I agree to a large extent with the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) that the ladies who are promoting this legislation could do more good by giving their attention to the matter of education than by seeking legislation on this subject. More can be done by the beneficial influence of women in teaching and educating our youth than in seeking legislation in this respect. The subject eu-91 r WILFRID LAURIER.
gaged the attention of parliament last year, and my hon. friend the Minister of Justice attempted to cope with it, but unfortunately) as he said himself at a later day, with very indifferent success. He introduced a measure which did not satisfy anybody, but he has been since looking into the matter. I am not prepared to say, however, that he has yet found a remedy. That something should be done goes without saying. Legislation to be effective should reach the man who supplies the noxious weed to tbe boys and prevent the sale to boys of tobacco in any form, but I do not see how we can undertake such legislation. It will be, hovf' ever, the duty of the government to apply itself further to this question, and perhaps at some later day my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will be able to give info1-' mation to the House on the subject'. The question is not a party one, and I think that the best interests of those who seek this legislation will be served by our not voting for this resolution.
